entry.title: Report: Claude Code sends users' email addresses in User-Agent headers during web searches, raising privacy concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Users have reported that Claude Code, an AI tool by Anthropic, includes their email addresses in the User-Agent request headers when performing web searches without their consent. This behavior has led to increased scam emails and privacy violations, prompting some users to switch to alternative platforms like Pi with OpenRouter. Anthropic introduced a built-in privacy mod in version 2.1.317 to block this behavior by default, which can be disabled via plugins. The issue has sparked significant discussion and criticism within the user community regarding the company's handling of privacy.

entry.title: Mark Cuban says Meta knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads generating $16 billion in fraud-linked revenue [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Mark Cuban accused Meta of knowingly allowing AI-generated deepfake scam ads on Facebook that target vulnerable users, including older adults, resulting in significant financial losses. Internal Meta documents revealed the company expected about $16 billion in revenue from ads linked to scams and prohibited products in 2024, with users seeing around 15 billion high-risk ads daily. Meta's internal safety staff estimated its platforms contribute to a third of successful scams in the U.S., with automated systems only banning advertisers when there is a 95% likelihood of fraud. Meta disputed the figures, stating complaints about scam ads had decreased and that it removed over 134 million scam ads in 2025. Older Americans reported losing $7.7 billion to internet crimes in 2025, with AI-related scams accounting for over $352 million in losses among reported cases. Cuban highlighted the cultural tolerance of such scams within Meta and urged users to be cautious of ads featuring famous faces, recommending verification and reporting suspicious activity to authorities. Meta has faced regulatory scrutiny, including an SEC investigation into advertising linked to financial fraud.

entry.title: Thinking Machines launches Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts AI model with vision input and improved agentic coding, available on Tinker with weights to be open-sourced after safety testing [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Thinking Machines introduced Inkling 2 Small, their second-generation AI model featuring 594 billion total parameters and 17 billion active parameters, supporting image inputs and variable effort. The model surpasses previous versions in performance on coding, vision, knowledge work, and reasoning tasks, achieving a score of 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Initially available through the Tinker platform with closed weights, the full model weights are planned to be released under an Apache 2.0 license following external safety evaluations. Inkling 2 Small incorporates a 292 million-parameter vision encoder and was trained with reinforcement learning on extensive long-horizon coding and autoresearch tasks, improving its ability to follow instructions, verify work, and perform autonomous research such as GPU kernel optimization. The model demonstrates strong visual reasoning and interpretation capabilities, including outperforming researchers in a wine tasting task using image inputs. It is accessible for fine-tuning and sampling on Tinker, with checkpoints to be downloadable upon weight release.

entry.title: Hungary releases communist-era secret police files revealing up to 60,000 former informants, granting public access for the first time
entry.summary: Hungary has made public secret police files from its communist era, identifying up to 60,000 informants as part of a long-delayed effort to confront its repressive past. The release follows a September bill by Prime Minister Peter Magyar that grants unrestricted public access to these records for the first time since the 1990 democratic transition. The disclosed documents include registration sheets, recruitment registers, and personal data of agents, accessible via an online search tool. The files reveal names of politicians, clergy, and public figures, alongside many lesser-known individuals. A second batch with more detailed information on about 9,000 informants is expected in February. The government has also set up support hotlines for those affected by the revelations. Hungary was under communist rule from 1949 to 1989, during which an estimated 150,000 agents were employed by the secret police, though only a fraction of their identities and activities are documented. The archives' director noted that the records are incomplete and not always reliable. The release marks a significant step in Hungary's ongoing political debate over transparency and reckoning with its communist history.

entry.title: Village's LLM Atlas shows closed AI models dominate the price-performance frontier across most budgets as of October 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Village's LLM Atlas maps the strongest AI models at every price point and finds that closed models now dominate nearly all budget ranges, with open models holding only about 3% mostly at the lowest cost tiers. This marks a significant decline from earlier in 2026 when open models held up to 41% of budgets, driven by releases like DeepSeek V4 Flash and Zhipu's GLM-5.2. The shift is attributed to closed labs' ability to distill cheaper models from their flagship offerings, release comprehensive model families covering multiple price points, and operate inference at large scale with cost efficiencies. Open models tend to win in bursts with strong, low-cost releases but are quickly undercut by closed models. The Atlas uses benchmark results and cost estimates from hosted APIs to evaluate models' capability and cost per task relative to GPT-5.

entry.title: Personal account of psychophysics experiences as a bilateral cochlear implant user
entry.summary: This article presents a personal perspective on psychophysics from the viewpoint of an individual using bilateral cochlear implants. It explores the sensory and perceptual experiences associated with hearing through these devices. The author discusses challenges and insights related to auditory perception and the impact of cochlear implants on daily life.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis to automate interpretable symbolic modeling of human and machine reasoning across hundreds of problems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers present Behavior-Conditioned Symbolic Synthesis (BCSS), a method for automatically generating interpretable symbolic programs that replicate human and machine reasoning behaviors across numerous challenging tasks. This approach addresses previous limitations in symbolic modeling caused by manual engineering and computational constraints. Analysis of the synthesized programs reveals common patterns in both humans and machines, such as oversimplification, partial rule adoption, and misinference of feature dependencies. These patterns vary with available cognitive resources, with reasoning effort influencing the degree of simplification and explanation. The findings suggest underlying satisficing mechanisms shared by humans and AI, and demonstrate BCSS as a tool for comparing rule-based reasoning between humans and black-box AI systems.

entry.title: Researchers introduce PromptOps, a framework for iterative prompt optimization to recalibrate large language models used as automated judges amid changing evaluation conditions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated judges to evaluate chatbots and AI systems, but their alignment with human evaluation policies can degrade over time due to shifts in user interactions and score distributions. Researchers propose PromptOps, a closed-loop framework that monitors and iteratively recalibrates LLM-as-a-Judge systems by deciding when and how to optimize prompts using various methods including GEPA, SIMBA, Rubric Synthesis, and exemplar selection techniques. Experiments show that iterative prompt optimization through PromptOps can recover LLM judge performance after controlled shifts in reference score distributions, though the effectiveness of optimization methods and timing varies by context. This work frames prompt optimization for deployed LLM judges as an ongoing maintenance challenge and offers PromptOps as a practical tool for studying and implementing this process.

entry.title: Researchers link information-theoretic empowerment and capability-based human power through goal revelation in Markov games, proposing a satisfaction floor to monitor user power in AI systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of measuring power in AI safety, focusing on how optimal agents tend to acquire power across various objectives, which risks human disempowerment in socio-technical systems. It compares two formal measures of power in Markov games: information-theoretic empowerment, which quantifies the influence of an agent's actions on future states, and capability-based individual power, which measures goal attainment probabilities for humans pursuing different goals. The authors introduce goal revelation, defined as the mutual information between a human's latent goal and the realized trajectory, and establish bounds linking it to empowerment and individual power using Fano's inequality. The study highlights potential failure modes where maximizing empowerment or revelation alone may not guarantee effective human goal attainment, such as preferring broad but irrelevant influence or failing to distinguish between functional and rewired interfaces. To address this, the authors propose a satisfaction floor computable from interaction logs to monitor retained user power in deployed systems. Simulations in random environments show that empowerment, revelation, and individual power are correlated but distinct quantities, underscoring the need for comprehensive measures to ensure human agency in AI-assisted environments.

entry.title: Researchers recover training data domains from LoRA fine-tuned model artifacts using classifiers on weights, activations, and outputs with up to 64% accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied whether the domain of training data used in Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning can be identified solely from the resulting model artifact without access to the original data. Using the Qwen3.5-0.8B base model, they produced 36 LoRA fine-tunes across 18 public datasets spanning five domains and extracted features from model weights, internal activations, and generated outputs to classify the training domain. The study found that domain classification accuracy reached 64% from black-box outputs and 61% from gray-box activations, outperforming white-box weight statistics at 42%, challenging the expectation that signal strength decreases from weights to outputs.

entry.title: Researchers introduce a behavioural framework to predict and understand loss of control in frontier AI systems using a composite score validated across 13 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed a behavioural framework to assess the risk of loss of control in advanced AI systems, which operate with diminishing human oversight and may act beyond effective human control. The framework breaks down risk into misaligned motive, harm-enabling capability, and monitoring evasion, combining 13 measurable aspects into a single loss-of-control (LoC) score that correlates strongly with failure rates in long-horizon risk scenarios across 13 frontier AI models. The study shows that risk varies across models and is not solely explained by capability, and demonstrates that targeted mitigations such as fine-tuning and enhanced monitoring can reduce failure rates while maintaining overall performance. This framework offers a practical approach for predicting, understanding, and mitigating loss-of-control risks in AI before they manifest.

entry.title: DictLLM introduces dictionary-based post-training compression for large language models, achieving 5.1x compression on LLaMA-7B with minimal performance loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: DictLLM is a new post-training compression method for large language models that decomposes weight matrices into a shared dictionary and sparse layer-specific coefficients without additional training. This approach reduces memory usage by sharing dictionaries across grouped layers and sparsifying coefficients, followed by aggressive quantization using Hessian-based information. On benchmarks including language modeling and zero-shot reasoning, DictLLM outperforms existing low-rank compression methods, compressing the LLaMA-7B model by 5.1 times with only a small increase in perplexity. This method offers a more efficient trade-off between model size and performance, enabling better deployment of large models on resource-constrained devices.

entry.title: RM-VLM uses large language and vision-language models to generate and ground reward machines from natural-language task descriptions for reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose RM-VLM, a method that combines a large language model to generate reward machines from natural-language task descriptions with a vision-language model to ground these reward machines over image observations during policy learning. This approach addresses the limitation of manually engineered labelling functions in reward machines, enabling handling of non-Markovian tasks in reinforcement learning. RM-VLM was evaluated on tasks including grid-world navigation, robotic manipulation, and 3D object collection, achieving higher success rates than existing vision-language model-based reward methods across all tested domains.

entry.title: Benchmarking five large language models on biomedical and cognitive knowledge graphs shows graph grounding reduces hallucinations and improves multi-hop reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated five large language models (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) on five heterogeneous knowledge graphs related to biomedicine and cognitive neuroscience. They tested reasoning depth and factual accuracy using a multitier query dataset under conditions with and without graph grounding, finding that general-purpose models generally outperformed domain-specific ones on complex reasoning tasks, and that graph grounding consistently reduced hallucination rates across all models. The study showed that domain-specific models do not always outperform general-purpose models without graph grounding, highlighting the benefit of combining broad language model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. The authors provide guidance on selecting integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints and discuss potential applications in personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI through hybrid neurosymbolic architectures.

entry.title: Researchers propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method that improves test-time reasoning efficiency by reducing token usage up to 41% while maintaining accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce StepBack, a method that enhances test-time reasoning efficiency by identifying and resampling likely error steps in reasoning trajectories. StepBack matches the accuracy of the widely used self-consistency decoding strategy across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks while significantly reducing token usage. The approach can also be combined with adaptive inference methods to further improve efficiency.

entry.title: Researchers build Scientist World, an executable research environment for AI-Scientists, releasing 1,000 verified paper-based environments and showing AI can surpass human researchers 74% of the time [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed Scientist World, a platform that transforms scientific papers into executable environments where AI-Scientists can conduct research and be evaluated against human results. The project includes 1,000 verified environments and records 6,400 hours of AI research activity, capturing ideas, experiments, and outcomes. This platform enables AI models to improve research ideation, with a small model achieving a 158% performance increase to match frontier AI researchers. Scientist World aims to provide AI-Scientists with a dynamic research ecosystem, growing alongside scientific progress.

entry.title: Researchers introduce BrainPFN, a meta-trained network for brain behavior prediction that outperforms Kernel Ridge Regression on small samples across four cohorts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: BrainPFN is a Prior Data Fitted Network designed to predict behavioral phenotypes from functional MRI data without requiring per-score or per-cohort refitting. It is meta-trained on a domain-specific prior built from approximately 7,000 real functional connectivity matrices, generating one billion synthetic training samples to enable efficient inference with a single forward pass. Across four independent cohorts, BrainPFN surpasses the performance of Kernel Ridge Regression, especially in small sample settings, and outperforms recent foundation models trained on datasets four to nine times larger. The researchers have publicly released their meta-training pool, code, and checkpoints, demonstrating that a modest, openly available dataset can match or exceed models trained on larger, restricted datasets such as the UK Biobank.

entry.title: Researchers benchmark frozen forecasting models as time series classifiers on MONSTER, finding limited gains over strong non-pretrained baselines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated two forecasting foundation models, Reverso and Chronos-Bolt, as frozen feature extractors for time series classification on six large MONSTER datasets using varying amounts of labeled data. They compared pretrained representations against four established classification methods and random-weight versions of the same models, finding that pretraining improved accuracy over random weights but did not consistently outperform the strongest non-pretrained baselines. The study showed that frozen pretrained representations performed worse than the best non-pretrained classifiers in most settings and only tied in a few cases. Additional experiments indicated that restoring amplitude information partially recovered performance, while fine-tuning and forecast-error features did not close the gap. These results emphasize the need for strong task-specific baselines and random weight controls when assessing forecasting foundation models for classification tasks.

entry.title: Researchers establish finite-time convergence and sublinear regret guarantees for neural reinforcement learning in finite-memory POMDPs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers address the computational challenges of reinforcement learning in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) by developing finite-time convergence and regret guarantees using nonlinear neural value function approximation. They establish a new finite-state MDP approximation error bound, prove a finite-time critic error bound via Temporal-Difference learning on superstate transitions, and combine these results with policy mirror descent to achieve sublinear regret against the optimal POMDP value. This work represents the first finite-time sublinear regret guarantee for neural function approximation in finite-memory POMDPs. Their numerical experiments support the theoretical findings.

entry.title: Researchers propose Mechanistic Shaping to train models to follow concept-based rules via internal representations, reducing targeted behaviors while preserving performance across domains and scales [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Mechanistic Shaping, a training framework that guides models to express and rely on specified concepts, such as avoiding harmful content or biased decision factors, by shaping their internal representations. The approach was tested across vision, medical imaging, and language tasks with models up to 32 billion parameters, showing substantial behavior reduction without harming task accuracy. The study also examines whether shaped concepts remain detectable, identifying three geometric mechanisms by which concepts can evade monitoring probes but finding that most shaped concepts remain monitorable with appropriate tools. These findings highlight the potential of interpretability techniques as training tools and call for rigorous methods in interpretability-based model training.

entry.title: A Night at the LLM Zoo: Data Conditioned Flow Matching for Generating Pretrained LLM Weights [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A challenge to Weight Space Learning as it expands from task specific and vision models to Large Language Models (LLMs) is the absence of a well curated and analyzed LLM population. To address this, we train such a model zoo for application to Weight Space Generation by systematically varying the data mixture composition between web text, books, mathematics, coding, and French across populations of 51M, 124M, and 355M parameter GPT-2 Models, each tier with count N = 100. We analyze these populations by cosine similarity, functional diversity, Leave-One-Mixture-Out modeling, and variance decomposition. We show that the zoo contains diverse models whose variation is structured by training mixture composition. We embed the training mixture composition to condition a Flow Matching model of complete pretrained LLM weights in Gram-PCA compressed weight space. By demonstrating zero-shot generalization to held out mixtures, measuring Continuous Ranked Probability Score skill, as well as finding minimal changes in downstream test-set perplexity and general capability benchmark scores, we show that our generator generalizes on the simplex of data mixtures to produce models that perform similarly to those in the zoo ex nihilo. Finally, we produce all source code and artifacts to support the continued expansion of Weight Space Learning and Generation into the LLM domain.

entry.title: Depth or Description? When a One-Step Latent Score Replaces Lookahead in Proactive Information Acquisition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A proactive agent must decide what to ask before it acts. Exact lookahead values combinations of questions but is expensive and leans on a fitted model; a one-step score is cheap but can miss them. Our main finding: the need for depth often lies in how the hidden cause is described. A one-step score on the label can be blind to an interaction among answers. A score on a suitable latent cause is not, and where that latent encodes the decision it replaces most of depth at a fraction of the search. Described differently, the same problem can defeat the score while exact values do not move, so keep the latent small and check it against exact values. Probabilities learned from one language model's answers do not carry to another unless planning allows for both; those read from tokens are worth only a few labels.

entry.title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07166v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Developers rarely give a coding agent a single request: they ask it to build a component and then to extend, upgrade, and optimize it, each time on code the agent itself wrote. Most benchmarks, however, score one task at a time. We introduce Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on a single codebase. Every step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code the agent produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward. The tasks span four families of engineering work and nine languages, include both from-scratch builds and existing open-source codebases, and ground every step in an existing source of truth that defines both the instruction and its verifier. Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model. We release Multi-step SWE publicly at https://multistepswe.com.

entry.title: Compositional Unalignment: Auditing Safety in Large Vision-Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) are vulnerable to compositional harm: an image and a prompt that are benign in isolation become harmful through the model's cross-modal reasoning. Recent alignment methods report strong scores on compositional safety benchmarks, but an LLM judge only measures observed behavior and cannot reveal how robustly safety is integrated into the model. We argue that un-alignment provides a complementary audit of alignment robustness. We first show that minimal supervised fine-tuning reaches an LLM-judge score comparable to a multi-stage reinforcement-learning pipeline, so similar benchmark scores cannot establish robustness by themselves. We then show that recognition and refusal of compositional harm are decoupled: nine standard direction-finding methods detect compositional harm with up to AUC=0.99, yet ablating the recovered directions either leaves refusal intact or destroys model coherence. We therefore propose CMaG, a training-free un-alignment method for compositional safety. CMaG measures refusal intention with a refusal-versus-compliance log-probability margin, takes its gradient with respect to mid-layer activations, and contrasts it against partially benign pairs to isolate the cross-modal interaction term. A single backward pass over 80 examples yields a direction along which steering monotonically converts refusal into compliance. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.5-7B, CMaG reduces compositional safety scores by up to 65 points while over 98% of outputs remain coherent, outperforming gradient-based baselines; the direction also transfers to text-explicit harm and un-aligns models hardened by defensive training. Compositional safety can thus appear behaviorally strong while remaining fragile to targeted internal intervention. Warning: this paper contains unsafe model outputs, including references to self-harm.

entry.title: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces large language model (LLM) deployment costs, but preserving quality requires accounting for uneven weight sensitivity. Uniform PTQ uses one weight bit-width, importance-aware PTQ adjusts scales or reconstructs weights within that width, and column-wise mixed precision retains selected columns at higher precision. However, sensitivity varies within columns, so whole-column retention also protects less sensitive weights, while runtime outlier detection adds decoding overhead. We therefore introduce TileQuant, a training-free framework that assigns precision to hardware-aligned 2D weight tiles. Offline calibration provides input-activation-aware scoring from forward statistics for lower calibration cost and gradient-informed scoring from loss sensitivity for stronger quality preservation. Within each projection's retention budget, the highest-scoring tiles remain at 16-bit and the rest use 8-bit. The resulting map guides reconstruction into compact weight buffers, which the kernel reuses for native integer and 16-bit computation with local accumulation to reduce memory traffic. Experiments show that TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput. Across language modeling, reasoning, long-context retrieval, and question answering, it preserves quality and surpasses quantized and original models on multiple tasks. These results support selecting precision units that capture local sensitivity while enabling efficient hardware execution. The implementation is: https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TileQuant

entry.title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.

entry.title: MAC-v2: Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study whether \emph{long-horizon model-based value expansion} can serve as an effective framework in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL). Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels is substantially harder than state-based environments, as the agent must learn both the representation and its dynamics, and errors from either can accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories. We introduce MAC-v2, which enables long-horizon model-based expansion from pixels by training a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. By learning representations from prediction and control objectives, MAC-v2 does not need to encode control-irrelevant visual details that can hinder the dynamics prediction. Action chunking further mitigates the prediction error by reducing the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion. Across diverse visual benchmarks including visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Our analyses show that long-horizon model-based value expansion is critical for the performance of MAC-v2, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.

entry.title: KG-Neighbor: Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Construction for Embedding Visualization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In embedding visualizations, nearby instances are interpreted as semantically related, although neighborhoods derived from input embeddings may not reflect content relationships. Neighborhood-based dimensionality reduction (DR) methods can propagate this limitation by optimizing layouts from embedding-based neighborhood graphs. We propose Knowledge-Guided Neighborhood Graph Construction (KGN), which represents relational knowledge derived from each instance as a set of knowledge graph (KG) triples. It uses the degree of triple sharing as pairwise semantic evidence to adjust embedding distances and reconstruct the top-k neighborhood graph; neither KG extraction nor neighborhood construction uses class labels. We also introduce IDProfile (IDP), which interprets residual mismatches by independently assessing whether the source content supports the assigned class label and the neighborhood-majority class. Across eight text and image dataset-encoder conditions, we characterize KGN over the full guidance-strength sweep and four KG similarity measures. Across this sweep, the maximum NMI and LT_2D each exceed the corresponding kNN baseline in all eight conditions, with the largest gains reaching 0.68 and 1.35, respectively. The gains and the extent of neighborhood reconfiguration vary across conditions and are larger under encoder conditions with lower kNN baseline scores. The IDP analysis shows that the largest reductions are concentrated in Placement Issue candidates, whereas Label Issue and Unresolved Case instances account for a larger share of the remaining review set. These results indicate that KGN can narrow the evaluated gap between embedding-based neighborhoods and content-supported semantic relations, while IDP shows that a residual mismatch should not automatically be interpreted as a projection failure.

entry.title: TriAttention: Unified Sparse Mixed-Precision Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparsity and quantization reduce the cost of attention by skipping interactions and lowering the precision of those retained. However, useful interactions differ in their precision requirements: some tolerate low-precision scores while remaining sensitive to removal. We therefore introduce TriAttention, which assigns query-key (QK) tiles to skipping, 4-bit, or 8-bit computation, using 4-bit to retain quantization-tolerant interactions at lower cost. To represent compactly, we encode each head's computation regions with two diagonal-distance boundaries, keeping policy storage independent of context length. Offline calibration then evaluates candidate boundary pairs using normalized projected-output errors and complete-tile execution costs. Using these measurements, a model-wide allocator selects each head's boundaries to minimize calibration error under a shared computation budget. During prefill, the selected boundaries generate precision-grouped traversals for a fused kernel that skips omitted tiles and combines contributions from both QK precisions into one normalized attention output. The quantized keys and values prepared during prefill are then reused in a compressed key-value (KV) cache for decoding, reducing repeated reads of prompt data. Experiments show that TriAttention achieves end-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over the Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline. Meanwhile, TriAttention maintains quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks. These results show how a compact retention-and-precision policy translates local sensitivities into attention computation and repeated KV-cache access. The implementation is https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TriAttention.

entry.title: Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood Learning: A Genetic Algorithm for Instance-Dependent k Optimization in Nearest Neighbor Classification [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07257v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The number of neighbours k is the central hyperparameter of the k-nearest neighbour (k-NN) classifier and is usually selected globally through cross-validation or evolutionary search. However, the bias-variance trade-off is inherently local: dense and noise-free regions may favour small neighbourhoods, whereas sparse or noisy regions may require larger ones. Since global-k optimization is one-dimensional, replacing exhaustive search with a genetic algorithm offers little computational advantage. We therefore optimize an instance-dependent neighbourhood policy instead. We propose EANK (Evolutionary Adaptive Neighborhood K), which uses a low-dimensional policy to map local neighbourhood descriptors, including density, label entropy, vote margin, and concentration, to an adaptive number of neighbours k(x). A real-coded elitist genetic algorithm optimizes this policy using leave-one-out accuracy with a neighbourhood-smoothness penalty. Precomputed neighbour votes reduce fitness evaluation costs. We investigate theoretical properties of the method, including dominance over global-k solutions on the training criterion, evolutionary convergence, policy regularity, and generalization guarantees. Experiments on synthetic data with spatially heterogeneous structure and twelve public datasets evaluate predictive performance, robustness, and computational cost. Under nested cross-validation, EANK achieves competitive performance relative to tuned global-k baselines and improves upon the default k=5. We also examine the gap between training and test performance to assess the practical value of adaptive neighbourhood selection.

entry.title: How Deep is the Signal? Time-Context up to 30 Years for Colorectal Cancer Prediction in a Primary-Care EHR Model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07265v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EHR foundation models read medical events within a fixed context window, and long context has so far been measured only in tokens. How far back in time a model must look to capture the earliest predictive signal is unknown. We introduce time-context, the calendar lookback window before the prediction point, and provide, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of decade-scale time-context for an EHR foundation model. We pretrained a decoder-only transformer (34.6M parameters) on 1.4B coded events from 3.6M primary-care patients in North West London and fine-tuned it to predict incident colorectal cancer under a 12-month pre-diagnostic buffer. A frozen cohort of 1,008 cases and 9,582 matched controls, all registered for at least 30 years, was evaluated at 15 nested lookback windows from 2 to 30 years, so that every truncation is compared within the same patients. Discrimination rose from an AUROC of 0.551 at 2 years to 0.590 at 18 years, then plateaued, with about 80% of the gain reached within 10 years; an XGBoost baseline converged to the same level (peak AUROC 0.589). A simulation further suggests that rotary position embeddings (RoPE) over elapsed time alias beyond about 20 years at the default base frequency, motivating a retuned $\theta$. Time-context is a measurable design axis for clinical prediction models, distinct from token-context, and should be reported.

entry.title: Satisficing as competitive Bayesian weighting: a minimal model of goal-directed choice under an unattained target [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Animals and humans often do not maximize; they act relative to goals (aspiration levels) that are frequently not yet met. How can a goal that is not (yet) realized organize choice? Deacon (2012) calls such absence-referenced organization \emph{ententional}, and Garc\'{i}a-Valdecasas and Deacon (2024) argue that ends are best understood as constraints rather than as particular states. We examine this idea in a minimal formal setting: Risk-sensitive Satisficing (RS), a bandit learning rule that values each action by its share of past trials multiplied by its surplus or shortfall relative to an aspiration level. We show that RS can be rewritten as a Bayesian-like estimator, Attention Competitive Bayes (ACB), in which the aspiration level is the prior mean of every action and the finite budget of trials sets how strongly evidence can override it. Two consequences follow. First, actions that are no longer sampled are partially overridden by the goal rather than by past observations: their estimates relax toward the aspiration level without any data being discarded. This ``pseudo-forgetting'' distinguishes ACB from models with an explicit forgetting rate. Second, when the aspiration is unattainable, exploration does not settle; in Bernoulli bandit simulations, adjusting the aspiration level from evidence reduced regret (expected loss). ACB offers an analyzable model in which an unattained goal and a limited attentional resource jointly constrain behavior, and it yields testable predictions about how organisms revalue options they have abandoned.

entry.title: Permanent and Transient Representations for Continual Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) agents struggle to adapt to new situations while retaining prior knowledge, leading to a stability-plasticity trade-off. One approach to solving this problem is by using complementary learning systems: one for slow, long-term learning and another for quick, transient adaptation. Anand & Precup (2023) instantiated this idea using permanent and transient value functions, but used the same features in both systems. Intuitively, long-term learning should rely more on parametric representations for broad generalization, while transient learning would be best served by non-parametric representations for situation-specific adaptation. In this paper, we explore this idea both theoretically and empirically. By introducing a novel non-parametric approximation for estimating the transient value function in complex tasks, we demonstrate that our method enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic, underscoring the effectiveness of our system-level decomposition.

entry.title: Test-Time Self-Play: Scaling without a Verifier [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-time scaling methods spend additional compute at deployment to improve a large language model's performance on a hard target problem. Most methods rely on a verifier that scores candidate solutions for correctness, using it to select among or refine the model's outputs. In many deployment regimes, however, a strong verifier on the target problem is unavailable. We introduce Test-Time Self-Play (TTSP), an approach to test-time scaling using asymmetric self-play without reliance on a verifier. On a difficulty-calibrated subset of LiveCodeBench v6, TTSP is the best-performing method at every verifier strength we evaluate, and the gap to the strongest baseline widens as the verifier weakens; in the no-verifier limit, TTSP yields a 35\% absolute improvement in mean@8. The gains hold across a range of verifier strengths, except when the base policy has near-zero coverage of the correct answer.

entry.title: IMUDINO: Self-distilled Foundation Model for Inertial Sensing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07437v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present IMUDINO, the first foundation model (FM) for inertial sensing to achieve competitive performance across diverse sensing tasks including human activity recognition (HAR), health, motion capture, and odometry. Prior inertial FMs often focus on one subfield of inertial sensing and sometimes underperform state-of-the-art supervised methods (e.g., in HAR), making their scope considerably narrower than FMs for vision and natural language. Moreover, they often require fixed input length and sampling rate, and generalize poorly to unseen sensor locations. To build a general-purpose foundation model for inertial sensing, we adapt the DINO self-supervised learning (SSL) paradigm to inertial data through a set of semantics-preserving motion transformations that simulate variations in motion pattern and sensor setup. For model architecture, we use a plain transformer encoder with frequency-aware positional encoding that natively supports varying input length and sampling rate. This simple setup proved remarkably effective for learning global and dense features generalizable across users, sensor setups, tasks, and, in the case of robot odometry, embodiments. We hope IMUDINO can serve as a backbone for inertial sensing and kickstart the development of general-purpose inertial FMs.

entry.title: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How can an agent handle a real-world task end to end? Frontier models with their own harnesses still fall short on real-world benchmarks: on Terminal-Bench 4.0, GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex resolves 37.3% of the tasks and Claude Opus 5 with Claude Code 51.8%. These tasks fail at the step from reaching a resource to applying it, which we call the last mile to the real world. Existing approaches put the resource within reach but leave the competence to apply it with the caller, so each harness rebuilds that competence. We introduce agent-native primitives, reusable units that equip a resource with a resident LLM that applies it in context and communicates with other primitives, and HEELO (Harness Engineering around Evolving Agent-Native Primitives for the Last Mile to Real-WOrld Tasks), a harness engineering framework that builds each task's harness from a library of such primitives. HEELO composes the primitives a task needs into a task-specific graph, verifies the result against evidence from the environment, revises the primitives a failure implicates, and admits new or improved primitives after validation. We instantiate HEELO with eight primitive families, each built for one kind of task, and evaluate them on more than twenty benchmarks. Dev-Primitives raise Terminal-Bench 4.0 resolution from 37.3% under Codex to 55.5% on the same backbone, Harness Primitives composed per task raise Terminal-Bench 2.0 Pass@1 from 60.0% for the seed harness to 72.2%, Tool Primitives raise ToolBench pass rate from 55.8% to 75.1%, and Navigation Primitives raise GAIA-Text-103 accuracy from 45.6% to 58.3%. On the 46 real-world tasks of our heelo.dev platform, Claude Opus 5.5 with Claude Code and GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex complete 9 each on their own and 39 and 35 when connected to HEELO through our MCP server, with 1.9$\times$ and 2.3$\times$ less time and 1.55$\times$ lower cost per completed task.

entry.title: Echoes of Error: Residual-Directional Local Rollout Consistency for Timeseries Forecasting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In time-series forecasting, rollout errors are not merely one-step fitting discrepancies: once fed back into the evolving state, they can perturb future predictions. We formalize this effect through local rollout consistency, which compares the next prediction produced under teacher forcing with that produced under free running. In principle, this consistency can be enforced directly by tracking the residual-induced perturbation of the next state. In practice, however, the residual-to-state alignment operator is often difficult to design when the input state and output block have different dimensions, heterogeneous components, or architecture-dependent layouts. We therefore use a first-order local surrogate that penalizes the Jacobian-vector product of the predictor along the actual feedback perturbation, suppressing precisely the directions through which self-generated errors remain visible to future predictions. We further give the same loss a geometric interpretation near a predictive manifold: by controlling residual-induced directions that probe the normal bundle, the objective yields theoretical conditions under which free-running trajectories remain inside a stability tube around the manifold. Experiments on time series forecasting tasks support this view, showing that the proposed regularization improves predictive accuracy. More broadly, our results suggest a training principle for time-series forecasters and sequential predictors: a model should not only make small one-step errors, but also learn not to let its own errors echo into the future. Code is available at https://github.com/Wangzzzzzzzz/Echoes-Of-Error.

entry.title: Adversarial Robustness of Kernel Machines: A Comprehensive Analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07474v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kernel machines are an important class of models in machine learning. However, the question of how robust modern kernel machines are to adversarial examples has not been studied comprehensively. In this paper, we provide a thorough empirical investigation of the adversarial robustness of kernel-based models for both binary and multiclass classification tasks, via white-box and black-box evasion attacks. We evaluate the native robustness of kernel machines, random feature classifiers, and the relatively newer Recursive Feature Machines. In addition, we provide an algorithm for approximate adversarial training of kernel machines. Our experiments on classification tasks on image and tabular datasets strongly indicate that kernel machines are natively more robust than neural networks, i.e., their performance degrades more gracefully against adversarial perturbations.

entry.title: KOSMOS: Self-scheduling Persistent Kernels for Communication-Compute Overlap [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07477v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tensor and sequence parallelism (TP+SP) and expert parallelism (EP) put collectives on the critical path of transformer layers. State-of-the-art fused kernels mitigate this with fixed roles or schedules, but this rigidity leaves large idle windows. Predicting a communication-computation split does not remove them either; a predetermined split cannot follow data readiness. We present KOSMOS, a library for self-scheduling persistent kernels whose workgroups use queues ordered by consumer demand to switch between communication and computation roles as data become ready, with no scheduler, per-call cost model, or tuned split. KOSMOS fuses every TP+SP collective of a transformer layer with its GEMM, and runs an entire expert layer, from router to fold, in one launch per direction. Evaluated on AMD Instinct MI350X and AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, KOSMOS speeds up TP+SP end-to-end training in Megatron-LM by 1.10-1.28x in BF16 and 1.10-1.25x in MXFP8. KOSMOS accelerates end-to-end training of DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen3-235B proxies by 1.29-1.83x over DeepEP.

entry.title: Localization Does Not Imply Steerability: A Mechanistic Study of Sign Errors in LLM Mathematics
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07478v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When large language models do multi-step mathematics, a characteristic failure recurs: the model writes one wrong sign token mid-computation -- a cofactor sign, the minus of a recursive integration-by-parts step -- then executes the rest of the arithmetic correctly, and the answer comes out wrong. We ask where inside the network that sign is written. Across six open models spanning 14B to 675B parameters, a per-layer readout shows the wrong sign is committed late -- by MLP layers in the last quarter of the network (70-100% per model and task), a pattern present, where tested (Qwen), in the base model before instruction tuning. The mechanism varies: some models carry fixed "minus-stamp" layers that push a minus regardless of the right answer, others carry amplifiers of whichever sign was already chosen, and Qwen adds a downstream rescue layer that opposes the stamp. The circuit is causal: subtracting a single sign direction from the residual stream flips 13 of 14 held-out minus-written integration-by-parts errors on Llama-3.3-70B, with flips replicating on Qwen, Gemma, and Mistral-Small (24-70% per cell), and with representation-level specificity -- the same dose breaks correctly-minus answers while sparing correct-plus answers where the direction is surgical (0/72 on Llama), and matched random-direction and control-layer interventions are null. Core claims were preregistered with pass criteria frozen in git before held-out data was seen: 23 of 29 checks passed, all misses reported. But causality is not uniform: Phi-4 implements an equally well-localized circuit at the same late depth, yet the identical intervention flips almost nothing -- the sign is written redundantly across ~15 layers with margins several times larger (median 17.8 logits). Localization, we conclude, does not imply steerability: two models can share a circuit location yet differ enormously in how overturnable it is.

entry.title: The Memory Trap: Language Agents Overgeneralize from Benign Interactions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07554v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language agents increasingly use persistent memory to record user preferences and procedures across sessions. We show that memory from benign interactions can cause unsafe or unreliable behavior on later tasks. We call this failure the memory trap. To study this issue, we compare behavior in sessions with and without memory across six frontier models (including Claude Sonnet, Opus, and Fable models and GPT-5.6). We evaluate these models in a range of settings. First, in autonomy experiments, we find that requests to skip confirmation during low-stakes coding chores lead agents to skip confirmation and verification on simulated high-stakes tasks in both coding and everyday life. We next study memories formed when users seek emotional support, or describe harm from uncritical feedback, and find these memories bias later judgments of mathematical work, arguments, and poems toward sycophancy or over-critique (respectively). Memory notes written during legitimate stale-test repairs lead agents to weaken correct tests that catch broken safeguards; these memories also increase cheating on ImpossibleBench, with larger increases for stronger Sonnet and Opus models. We show that memory traps can arise both from overgeneralizations in memory writing, and when acting on memory. These findings demonstrate that even benign interactions can lead to serious risks from memory systems, and thus motivate the need for new research into ensuring that agents preserve the scope of their memories.

entry.title: Stress Testing Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Against Covert Misalignment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07586v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLM agents advance rapidly in autonomy, the risk of hidden objectives that bypass safety constraints becomes increasingly plausible. Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring offers a key control mechanism by reading the agent's reasoning and flagging misalignment before it materializes into action, yet its reliability depends on the realism of the red-team it is stress-tested against. Existing red-teaming efforts rely on shared templates, such as casting a side task as a prerequisite, which treat the side objective as an exogenous insertion and leave task-specific, contextually grounded evasions underexplored. We therefore ask: How robust is CoT monitoring against agents that strategically conceal misalignment? To answer this, we introduce TraceMRT, an automated Trace-level Monitor Red-Teaming framework that reframes the side task as a coherent sub-goal of the primary task and searches trace-shaping strategies whose induced trajectories complete the misaligned objective while reading as natural execution. Through black-box attacks on state-of-the-art monitors such as GPT-5.2 and Claude-4.5, we reveal substantial vulnerabilities even in top models. To counter these vulnerabilities, we propose a Bayesian Trajectory Monitoring framework, integrating global context and local segment evidence to detect covert misalignment. Empirically, our method significantly consolidates monitor robustness with 0.91 AUC and 0.74 TPR@FPR=0.05.

entry.title: Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07589v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities. Moreover, she commits to nonnegative payments and provides recommendations and contexts, but receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback. We develop halving-type algorithms that learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, achieving a sample complexity of $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ that matches worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We then combine these learning procedures with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation, and steering toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria (EFCE). With high probability, the Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves a directness gap and an optimality gap of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/4})$, while time-average payments are of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/8})$.

entry.title: Measuring the Marginal Value of Verifier-Based RL Beyond Supervised Fine-Tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is usually evaluated as an alternative to supervised fine-tuning (SFT), or as a stage that follows it, with the implicit assumption that the RL stage contributes gains of its own. We measure that contribution directly, in a controlled setting where both stages can be run to completion and compared exactly. We built gpu-train-debug, a deterministic benchmark of 1,877 synthetic GPU and LLM training failure diagnosis tasks across 30 archetypes, graded by a programmatic verifier with partial credit, and calibrated so that a mid-tier model scores in a 0.60 to 0.75 band. A pilot produced a surprise: 1,200 gold demonstrations nearly solved the benchmark (SFT 0.785 on the hard split), while 15 steps of GRPO from the base model did not move it (0.314 vs 0.311 base). We therefore amended the study, in writing and before the full run, to ask the sharper question: what does verifier-based RL add beyond demonstrations? At the pre-registered scale (60 GRPO steps, learning rate 1e-6), the answer is: no detectable improvement in-distribution (+0.22 points, 95% CI [-0.06, +0.51]), and a modest but measurable improvement under distribution shift (+0.33 points on a held-out OOD split, CI [+0.02, +0.68]). SFT accounted for most of the available improvement, while verifier-based RL produced only modest additional gains under distribution shift. The residual errors SFT leaves are mostly systematic, identical across samples, which likely reduces the within-group learning signal available to GRPO. A full 60-step cold-start GRPO arm confirms the pilot at the full horizon. The whole study cost $8.69 of compute and is fully reproducible from archived generations, frozen configs, and tagged code.

entry.title: WaSP: Wasserstein Data Synthesis Pipeline for Solver-Free Operator Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural operators offer fast surrogates for solving PDEs, but training them typically requires expensive input-solution pairs. Two solver-free alternatives include physics-informed learning and training on manufactured data. Physics-informed learning approximates solutions by minimizing PDE residuals. While the residual norm must be strong enough to control solution error, stronger norms increase mini-batch variance and hinder optimization. Manufactured data constructs input-solution pairs for learning by applying the PDE operator to artificial solutions. However, the resulting training distribution can be mutually singular with the target distribution, yielding poor accuracy on the target distribution. We introduce the Wasserstein Data Synthesis Pipeline (WaSP), which trains on manufactured input-solution pairs while gradually mitigating the distribution shift. WaSP synthesizes new pairs by applying the learned operator to a path of intermediate distributions converging to the target input distribution. Training proceeds in stages along this path. At each stage, the previous surrogate generates solutions, and the exact PDE operator derives corresponding inputs, yielding training pairs for the next surrogate. Theoretically, we prove a stepwise error-propagation bound for the distribution shift introduced during synthesis. Empirically, WaSP reduces solution error by $3.9\times$ to $9.5\times$ compared to existing solver-free methods on PDEs such as Allen-Cahn, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, and Ginzburg-Landau, and better reproduces the two chaotic systems' statistical observables.

entry.title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.

entry.title: InfMasking: A Unified Variational Framework for Synergistic Multimodal Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07702v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal models are expected to exploit synergistic information, that is, information available only when multiple modalities are observed together. In practice, however, a fusion module can fit the training objective by relying on a dominant modality or on information that modalities share, and the synergy between modalities is often left unused. We propose InfMasking, a unified multimodal learning framework based on Infinite Masking. Before fusion, InfMasking randomly masks the features of each modality; each sampled mask produces a different partial combination of cross-modal evidence and a fused representation of the corresponding modality interactions. All masked fused representations are required to remain consistent with a reference target: the unmasked fused view when training is unsupervised, and the class proxy of the task label when labels are available. Maintaining this consistency across diverse partial combinations discourages reliance on a dominant modality or on shared information alone, and drives the fusion module to learn cross-modal interaction patterns that remain meaningful under partial observations. Since the objective is an expectation over infinitely many masks, we model the masked fused representations as Gaussian and optimize closed-form variational bounds, whose population-moment gaps are controlled by the masking-induced covariance under this model. On the evaluated benchmarks, InfMasking improves predictive performance and yields higher mean PID estimates of task-label synergy in learned modality-specific representations, alongside higher InterSHAP interaction attribution in the trained predictors. Code is available at https://github.com/brightest66/InfMasking.

entry.title: Evaluating Language Model Features for Zero-Shot Time-Series Anomaly Detection Under Isolation Assumption [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) is a fundamentally challenging task: it is unsupervised, requires high local precision capabilities, and suffers from limited labelled data. Recent work has explored adapting Large Language Models (LLMs) to time-series via cross-modal transfer. However, existing approaches are poorly suited to Multivariate TSAD (MTSAD), as tokenisation often obscures fine-grained temporal and variables structures, and most methods optimise auxiliary objectives such as forecasting or reconstruction. We posit that these surrogate objectives become unreliable as model capacity increases. Highly expressive models risk reconstructing or forecasting anomalies, undermining the foundations of both strategies. Instead, we propose to use LLMs purely as feature extractors and directly analyse their induced feature spaces. In this work, investigate the ability of LLMs to provide useful representations for MTSADs in a zero-shot setting through classification. To this end, we study the separability of the extracted features, under the assumption that anomalous features should be isolated from normal ones. We analyse their temporal and contextual discriminative ability using simple step-wise tokenisation schemes, with one time-step per token, which preserve fine-grained local information. Their usability for MTSAD is assessed using an unsupervised Isolation Forest, enabling a direct evaluation of the resulting representation quality. We further investigate whether the observed performance can be attributed to the language-related pre-training of the LLMs or arises independently of it. Our results provide empirical insight into the ability of LLMs to represent multivariate time-series for anomaly detection and highlight broader applications of cross-modal foundation models.

entry.title: Extending Reasoning in Typed Decision Models via Looping [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07736v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Typed decision models choose among a fixed set of answer options in a single forward pass, so unlike generative language models they cannot spend more test-time compute on hard inputs by generating more tokens. Looping a block of layers offers this compute in latent space without adding parameters, but prior work found no gain from loops retrofitted into conventionally pretrained models. We show that such loops help when trained together with the decision model. Our method, RELOAD (retrofitted loops for adaptive decisions), fine-tunes a pretrained encoder or decoder with a damped loop over its middle block and a lightweight controller picks the number of passes adaptively for each input. Across six models from 0.4B to 4B parameters, looping improves both accuracy and calibration, mostly on problems that need longer chains of reasoning than any seen in training, where encoders gain up to 23 points. Neither matched training compute nor more data closes this gap, and separate layers for each pass come close only with nearly twice the parameters. The controller keeps most of the gain at about three quarters of the compute.

entry.title: Scaling Laws for SAE Training Data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation storage is often a bottleneck in sparse autoencoder (SAE) training. We study how many unique activations an SAE needs when its total training budget is fixed. Quality improves rapidly as the buffer grows, then reaches a plateau where replaying the buffer is nearly as effective as using fresh activations throughout training. Beyond this point, additional unique activations bring little benefit to reconstruction or interpretability, so the buffer need not grow with the training budget. We describe this tradeoff between diversity and repetition with a scaling law for limited data. We validate it across dictionary sizes and token budgets, early, middle, and late layers of Llama-3.1, Qwen3 model sizes, and BatchTopK, TopK, and JumpReLU SAEs. Sweeps using mathematical text and Python code test the effect of changing the activation source. Evaluation covers explained variance (EV), reconstruction MSE, feature absorption, automated interpretability, and sparse probing. These results give a practical training rule: choose the smallest buffer that reaches the quality plateau and replay it for the remaining budget. In our experiments, this reduces activation storage by $8\text{--}64\times$ with negligible quality loss.

entry.title: Masked diffusion as random sequential adsorption: an exactly solvable model for parallel decoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07845v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Masked diffusion models generate text by reversing a stochastic masking process. Unlike autoregressive LLMs, which generate text one token at a time, they can reveal many tokens in parallel, at the price of an error, since tokens revealed together are drawn independently. We show that this trade-off maps onto the statistical physics of driven many-particle systems. (i) For any data, the error of parallel generation is the entropy production of the generation process relative to the reversed masking process. (ii) For Markov data, generation is a random sequential adsorption process with labelled gaps, which we solve exactly for any number of steps. (iii) For many steps, the error becomes the dissipation of a slowly driven system: the unmasking schedule plays the role of the driving protocol, the number of steps that of its duration, and the error is set by a thermodynamic metric that we obtain in closed form from the mutual information between tokens. Optimal schedules are geodesics of this metric. The exact solution shows how correlations in the text shape both the error and the quality of the output. The longer the correlations, the more the error concentrates at the start of generation. Schedules that start with small steps then gain more, both in path error and in perplexity, and need fewer steps to reach their asymptotic behaviour.

entry.title: Computation, not weight access: large language models as auditors of clinical prediction networks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have been reported to read, edit and write the weights of small neural networks, raising the prospect of auditing clinical prediction models from their files alone. Public demonstrations, however, mixed reading raw weights with running code. We separated these conditions in internally pre-specified simulation experiments. Tanh networks of 105 to 38,401 weights were trained on simulated cohorts of patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage, each with a planted relationship or none, and one network was trained on labels that under-recorded deaths in a subgroup. GPT-6 Astra and four other GPT models answered single prompts under a default or an explicit system instruction, either with the weights in the prompt and no tools, or with a calculation-only tool that exposed the weights (white box) or only the network's predictions (black box). Without tools, Astra recovered planted relationships in 353-weight networks but became unreliable at 3,457 weights, and under the default instruction it declined 11 of 12 audit and repair tasks as unidentifiable; the explicit instruction removed these refusals. With the tool, it recovered the planted relationship in all 29 runs on networks of up to 38,401 weights, raised no false alarm in 15 runs on null networks, and found the biased subgroup in 6 of 6 runs. Black-box access performed as well as white-box access, and other GPT-6 models read as accurately. A well-designed script matched the comparator models on the audit and the best LLM repair. For auditing these networks, what mattered was computation and elicitation, not access to the weights.

entry.title: When, Where, How: Active In-Context Learning for Tabular Foundation Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) adapt to a new task only through the labeled rows in their context. However, labels are expensive to acquire in real-world scenarios due to the need for highly specific domain knowledge to ensure high-quality data. Active in-context learning transfers classical acquisition rules to this setting, in which the model that guides acquisition changes with every label added. We ask how the value of diversity, predictive uncertainty and target-aware information gain changes as a frozen TFM acquires more context. For that, we study Target-Aware Nearest Neighbor (TANN) acquisition and the Expected Predictive Information Gain in Context (EPIC) and evaluate them against classical rules. Our study across twenty benchmarks with two well-established TFMs and classical GBDTs highlights three findings: (i) When: diversity-based acquisition is best during the first acquisition iterations; (ii) Where: labeling pool rows that serve the target inputs via a simple target-aware nearest-neighbor rule matters substantially; (iii) How: EPIC yields the best models at the label budget, retains on average 80--87% of the chance-corrected full-data performance with only 5-10% of the pool labeled on the eight benchmarks with the largest pools, and selects labels that also improve the predictive performance of gradient-boosted decision trees.

entry.title: DISCERN: Distributional Synthetic Replay for Retain-Free Incremental Machine Unlearning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a trained model without retraining from scratch. In real deployments, however, deletion requests arrive over time, calling for incremental class unlearning (ICU): classes are removed sequentially, previously forgotten knowledge must remain forgotten, and the remaining classes must be preserved. We present DIstributional SynthetiC rEplay for Retain-free iNcremental unlearning (DISCERN), an intervention-based class unlearning method that replaces access to the retain set with synthetic embeddings sampled from per-class parametric distributions. Unlike prototype-based replay, which assumes an isotropic Gaussian around each class centroid, DISCERN fits Euclidean (Gaussian, Laplace, Student's $t$) and directional (von Mises--Fisher, Fisher--Bingham) families to each class and selects among them through statistical tests and, when none of them accepts, cross-validated log-likelihood. This design is motivated by the architecture-dependent latent geometry: transformer embeddings lie approximately on a hypersphere and concentrate around class directions, unlike those of convolutional networks. We evaluate DISCERN against seven retain-free baselines on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 with two convolutional and two transformer backbones, under single-class, multi-class, and incremental unlearning. DISCERN is competitive when classes are removed at once and is the most stable method in ICU on transformers: on ViT-B/16, after 20 sequential deletions it retains a harmonic mean of $0.797$, whereas the strongest method in the simultaneous setting drops from $0.918$ to $0.048$. A paired ablation shows that per-class distribution selection substantially reduces the resurfacing of previously forgotten classes, acting as a stabilizer of accumulated forgetting rather than a uniform improvement.

entry.title: Structure from Collision via Hypothesis-Space Reasoning
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07900v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge of the hidden interior structure of an object, including the presence and location of cavities, is essential for predictive simulation, robotic manipulation, and nondestructive inspection. However, such cavities leave no direct signature on the static visible surface, making collision-induced deformation one of the few cues used to infer their presence. Structure from Collision (SfC) addresses this problem by recovering the hidden interior structure of an object from multiview observations of a collision event. SfC is challenging for two reasons: hidden cavities are only indirectly observable through surface motion, and voids correspond to the absence of material, making direct optimization using standard density representations difficult. The density-based SfC baseline inherits both difficulties. Surface-matching gradients do not directly indicate the cavity location, while density gradients can be weak or uninformative inside or near void regions. Therefore, we reformulate SfC as hypothesis-space reasoning, representing hidden cavities as explicit structural hypotheses whose variables encode available structural assumptions rather than relying on implicit density updates. A global stage performs gradient-free optimization over this hypothesis space using forward-only material point method (MPM) simulation. A local stage then refines the selected hypothesis as a Lagrangian particle system through gradient-based optimization using differentiable MPM simulation. On the SfC benchmark, our method improves hidden-structure reconstruction and future prediction over the density-based SfC baseline. Interior-topology stress tests and robustness analyses characterize its scope and limitations. The project page is available at https://www.kecl.ntt.co.jp/people/kaneko.takuhiro/projects/sfc-hypothesis/.

entry.title: AttnSR: Attention Step Reward for Long-Horizon Agentic RL [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.07932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents make multi-step decisions, yet outcome-reward-only reinforcement learning provides little direct supervision for individual steps. We introduce AttnSR, a step-level reward augmentation method that derives reward allocations from policy attention extracted during training replay, without a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts. AttnSR traces backward through the policy model attention graph to estimate the relevance of earlier steps to the final response. The terminal step, measured relative to a running baseline, determines whether these rewards reinforce or penalize the selected steps. In a controlled Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct study, AttnSR consistently outperforms the PPO baseline across all evaluated checkpoints on ALFWorld, raising final held-out success from 91.2% to 97.1%. The ablation experiment shows that the benefit depends on how intermediate rewards are assigned, rather than simple accumulation of step rewards over time. AttnSR also improves ScienceWorld at every checkpoint while cutting environment interactions by 29.9%. These results support policy attention as a practical prior for step-level reward allocation in long-horizon agentic RL. Code is available at https://github.com/fairyshine/AttnSR .
